en: This stage of completion (*utpannakrama*) and the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*) do not exist without initiation (*abhiṣeka*), and that [initiation] does not exist without a mandala; therefore, he explains them according to the ritual procedure, beginning with "Now," and so forth. The remainder of the sentence is: "I shall fully explain the ritual procedure of the mandala. It should be understood that the procedure by which the disciple is initiated is also being proclaimed.

"First, as one whose nature is the deity": having performed the preliminary service through the cultivation of the three samādhis, being the embodiment of Śrī Vajradhara; "HŪṂ"—this refers to the syllable HŪṂ. "The transformation into a vajra" means the visualization of a vajra produced from HŪṂ extending from the soles of the feet down to the bottom of the earth. "With effort" refers to that which will be described below. "Divine dust" refers to precious gems; "middling" refers to rice and the like.

"Four" (catur) means three cubits plus three finger-breadths on each of the four sides; thus is the mandala indicated, which he will explain in the twenty-eighth [chapter]. In that regard, the consecrations such as the garland and water are easily understood from other tantras in detail, and should be known here as well. And so it has been said:
"In this ritual, there are no specific ritual procedures of one's own."
In that regard, the wise rely upon the procedure taught in the general tantras.

Thus. Briefly stated, introducing the practice for the purpose of accomplishing the maṇḍala and for the purpose of initiation, he says: "The Vidyās," and so forth. The divine, supreme Vajrayoginīs are to be introduced. Are these to be cultivated solely for the sake of initiation? No; because of the words "the mantra," and so forth. The mantra-path is the mantra-system.

The Vajradevī is the sovereign of infinite world-realms. At the time of initiation, she is to be cultivated even at other times by relying upon the state of self-consecration, which is the state of non-dual great bliss. The *samaya* is the experience of great bliss, as explained previously.

"From the perspective of ultimate reality" (*paramārthataḥ*): the "ultimate" (*parama*) is the experience of the continuous flow of unsurpassed, untainted great bliss (*anāsrava-mahāsukha*). "Reality" (*artha*) means purpose; it refers to that [experience] and its cause. This is difficult to transgress even for Vajrasattva and others, let alone for others. And this alone is the established tenet (*siddhānta*). For it is said:
"In the mandala, in the observance, in the time, in the convention of mantra and mudrā..."
And regarding the deity and the Siddhānta, the Samaya was taught by the Jinas.

"For this purpose" means for the purpose already stated; for even consecration has that very purpose. Having indicated "one should approach," he will specify [the recipient] by means of the offering of wisdom (*prajñā*). He shows the mundane and supramundane conduct consisting of that *vajra*, which is the *bodhicitta*; thus, he is the *vajrācārya*, the Guru. "An ocean of qualities":

because he has been consecrated and authorized by the Guru according to the ritual rules, his qualities consist of compassion, faith, learning, reflection, the knowledge of the distinctions regarding the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), and so forth, as well as the realization of profound reality and the thorough knowledge of the ten realities. (Bhavabhaṭṭa?)
The maṇḍala, one’s own meditative absorption, the forming of mudrās, the seat, the recitation, the fire-oblation, as well as the worship, and the withdrawal through the yoga of ritual action—
thus [it is said].

The protective rites, consecrations, the varieties of offerings and recitations, the practice of the *pratyaṅgirā* mantra, the accomplishment of the mandala, the application of forceful methods (*haṭha*), and the ritual dismissal.
Thus, the ten principles (*tattva*) have been stated; they will be explained in their proper place.

As for wisdom (*prajñā*), he says that in the absence of divine [wisdom], others may also serve; this is expressed by the words "or else" (*atha vā*) and so forth. "With her" (*tām*) means together with her; she is the means for accomplishing innate bliss (*sahajasukha*).

"Girls" (*kanyā*): their status as girls is due to their being unenjoyed. In that regard, according to the sequence to be described, one who is truly unenjoyed should be taken for the *vidyā-vrata*. However, in the case of the mandala-sādhana and so forth, in the absence of such [a girl], even one who has not yet menstruated may be taken immediately after the onset of menses; and even in the absence of that, one who has not been enjoyed on that very day may be taken. Their status as girls is also due to their being childless and the presence of youth. "Priceless" (*anargha*) means "beyond value"; this indicates their rarity and their worthiness of worship through supreme love.
"Family lineage" (*kulakrama*) refers to the lineage beginning with Vairocana and the others.

"Sixteen years old" is stated because youth is the primary factor; this statement is also applicable to the mother when circumstances permit. For this very reason, it says "endowed with fresh youth. In her absence, another may also be used. Thus, for instance, from twelve to twenty years of age, nine mudrās are generally considered superior for all mandalas or for every yogin. From twenty-five years of age onwards, they are middling mudrās; those beyond that are inferior. As it is said in the *Mahāmudrātilaka*:
From the *Mahāmudrātilaka* (Chapter 23), test; *Vajrāvalī* 62 (176v/354):
"One who has reached twenty-five years of age should be accepted, while the others should be rejected.
However, it is stated that one who is eleven years old is beneficial for alchemy (*rasāyana*).

The three refuges are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Taking refuge is the wisdom that consists in the absolute acceptance of these as one’s own refuge, which is not to be transgressed; this is the secret of reality (*tattvarahasyam*). "Reality" (*tattva*) and "secret" (*rahasya*) refer to the commitments (*samaya*) and so forth. Now, is he who speaks thus the very Guru? And may that disciple, desiring to sport with that Guru, enter into union with him or not? She may indeed do so. Thus it is said in the *Vajrārallitantra*:
Having abandoned doubt, as well as laughter and derision,
O Goddess, one should not conceal the primary amorous play with the Guru.
One should delight the Guru in the "man-like" posture, which bestows all fruits.
One should always look upon the guru with passion; then, taking the guru’s phallus (liṅga) with the right hand and placing the vulva (bhaga) into the guru’s hand,
one should recollect the mantra of the vidyā.

Always taking that essence and having prepared a sacrificial oblation (caru), one should consume it. O fair-faced one, the accomplishments (siddhis) proclaimed by me in various tantras are obtained when the Guru is satisfied; therefore, the Guru should always be propitiated.

(177v/356) Sound consists of the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) and *hāsya* (comic) sentiments interwoven with refined (*saṃskṛta*) and vernacular (*prākṛta*) languages, as well as the warbling of pigeons and other birds. The lower path consists of a man’s skill in assuming lower postures and gazing at the lotus [of the vulva]. The reality of the tongue is proficiency in stimulating the *vajra* and the pericarp of the lotus with the tongue, as well as in drinking the honey from the mouth and so forth. For when the beloved is full of passion, she attains bliss by being herself full of passion upon seeing him. The upward projection is the specific arrangement of hands and feet during the *puruṣāyita* (man-like) position.

And there is the mutual gazing of eyes upon faces; the kissing of the eyes and so forth; the three-syllable [marks], nail-scratches, *ācchuritaka*, and so on; the grasping of the breasts with the right hand while the neck is bound with the *vajrabandha* posture; and various other acts such as the *utphullaka* and so forth.

In that [utphullaka pose], having placed the front half of the body in a low position and the rear half in a high position, the woman's knees are on the man's belly, her feet on his back, and her feet are bent down below the middle of the woman's buttocks; with her arms clinging to the man's sides, the man has his two arms clinging to the woman's back—this is the *utphullaka*. The woman has her shanks doubled and turned upward, while the man has his limbs made straight.

The *viṣamasaṃpuṭa* (uneven casket) occurs when the woman’s feet are on the man’s buttocks and they embrace each other’s necks. When the woman lies supine, her shanks are under the man who is seated; the woman’s arms are around the man’s neck, the man’s hands are at the woman’s sides, and the woman’s feet are at the man’s sides—this is the vulgar (*grāmya*) variety.

When the woman’s two knees have reached her own region and her shanks are extended, her feet are pressed against the sides of the man’s body; when the man’s hands are at the woman’s neck, and the woman’s hands are outside the man’s knees on the bed—this is the *nāgaraka* (the urban style). When the man, holding the feet of the supine woman, encircles her neck with his arms, and the woman’s hands are upon the man’s buttocks—this is the *ūrusphoṭa* (thigh-breaker).

One foot is on the chest and the second is extended; the hands are clasped behind the back—this is the *puruṣahasta* (man’s hand) position, [used] when a woman’s waist is extended. When the feet of a supine woman are extended outside the bed, and likewise the feet of the seated man are extended outside the bed; the man’s hands are clasped around the woman’s neck and the woman’s hands are clasped behind the man’s back—this is the *sūcī* (needle) position.

When a woman, remaining standing, takes delight as she revolves like a potter’s wheel—lifting her pair of feet again and again, placing her left hand upon her right elbow and her right hand upon her left elbow—it is called *bhramaraka*.

When a woman sits facing a supine man, blocking the expanse of the sky with the tips of her two raised feet, and making his shanks her seat, she delights him while her arms are locked around his neck and his arms are pressed against her back; this is the *madanatoraṇa*. When a woman stands upon the two extended and bent feet of a seated man, with her own two feet bent, and delights him by churning him, it is called *manthana*.

In this way, other instruments (*karaṇa*) as well should be understood by those devoted to them elsewhere. For it is through these instruments that yoginīs come to experience the taste of the great bliss of sexual union (*surata-mahāsukha-rasa*) by means of making the body supple. What is the purpose of this exertion? It is for the sake of accomplishment (*siddhi*). The sense is that when wisdom (*vidyā*) has been purified through the practice of the two sequences thus explained, or by the placement of the digits of the five families (*pañcakula-kalā-nyāsa*), it becomes the cause for the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā-siddhi*), let alone for other accomplishments.

Therefore, the Vidyādhara, endowed with his own wisdom, should offer this refined knowledge (*saṃskṛtavidyā*) and address the Guru as follows: "Out of compassion, you should accept this in order to grant me initiation. Having asked what he should do, [the text] says: "With perfumes," and so forth. Here, "milk" refers to wine; "mudrā" refers to the female practitioner (*sādhikā*). The meaning is that she too should perform acts of hospitality and the like. It is called "having emptiness as its core" because it is born from emptiness. "The gnoses of the Omniscient One" refers to the powers (*bala*), the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), and so on. Because its form is the perfectly pure gnosis, it is called the "embodiment of gnosis" (*jñānamūrti*).

Having thus praised him in the form of Akṣobhya, he praises him in the forms of Vairocana and the others, beginning with the word *jagat*. The meaning is that the reality (*tattva*) which is pure due to the removal of the stains of the two obscurations is the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Vajrasattva is the essence of mirror-like wisdom.
Bodhicitta is the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), [the nature of] Ratnasambhava.
Because he has conquered all adversaries through the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), he observes the world; thus Amitābha is the "Hero of the World" (*jagadvīra*).

Because he fulfills the command to perform deeds for the benefit of sentient beings for the Vajradhara, he is the "Executor of the Sugata’s Command. Śrī is the performance of duties; because he possesses that through identity with it, he is Amoghasiddhi. Because he is generated by the Vajradhara, he is a "Son of the Buddha.
The unsurpassed reality is the fourth consecration. The vajra is the conventional and ultimate bodhicitta. By means of that, the consecration which occurs in the vase and so forth is [meant].
The secret is the reality that is not within the sphere of the śrāvakas and others. To him, Vajradharmī Vajragarbha, having given the consecration—just as it was said:
“Hevajratantra (II.v.42cd):
‘In order to bestow the initiation upon Vajragarbha, Tilottamā was summoned.
Regarding the word “then” (*tataḥ*): it refers to [the stage] following the request made after first performing worship and the offering of the *vidyā*.

"Five": they are called *kāmāḥ* (desires) because when not yet obtained, they are desired or longed for; they are called *guṇāḥ* (qualities) because once obtained, they are cultivated and enjoyed again and again. Thus, *kāmaguṇāḥ* (objects of desire) refers to both desires and qualities. These are the excellent forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. Their quality of being desirable belongs to both the foolish and the yogins. "In yoga" means by a yogin.

The *mudrā-yoga* (182v/366) is the meditative union (*samāpatti*) with the consort offered by the disciple. In the "lotus-vessel," that is, within the *dharmodayā*, the *bodhicitta*—the semen—is [visualized]. Regarding the phrase "born from the Victor" (*jinātmaja*): having attracted the Tathāgatas via the rays of light from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, their very self—the body—together with Prajñā, melts through the festival of great bliss. Having entered within through the door of Vairocana and emerged via the path of the *vajra*, one should visualize it sprinkling the disciple seated upon the lotus. Then, [the drops] born from that, having issued forth from the lotuses and remaining in the sky...

The Guru, who is the Lord of the World and the embodiment of Vajradhara, should confer initiation upon the disciple—who has emerged from the lotus and is joined with the wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā)—while he is being consecrated by the Tathāgatas, the Vidyās, and the goddesses.

"Excellent jewel" refers to the vase initiation (*kalaśābhiṣeka*), which is the cause of supreme delight. It is "delightful" because it is the cause for the deity's empowerment and protection, among other things. It is "divine" and "supreme" for those practicing the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) because it brings about immortality; however, for those established in the completion stage (*utpannakrama*), it is naturally purified.

Mahārakta is menstrual blood. Karpūra is human flesh, marrow, fat, or hard phlegm. Red sandalwood is feces, because it colors and gladdens by nourishing body and mind. Vajra-water is urine. That which arises from the mind is semen. And it is said in the *Samājottara*:
"By its very nature, the five impurities shine forth among the bodily constituents."
"Because they are empowered by the five wisdoms, they are known as the five nectars. Thus, "samaya" refers to the five nectars.
"Killing living beings" is an indicative term for other types of misconduct.

He introduces the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*). "As previously mentioned" refers to that [consort] who was offered by the disciple. "Fashioned" means in the form of a goddess. "Pervaded by *sihlaka* and camphor" means possessing abundant pollen and semen. As it says in the *Samājottara*: "Having made her filled with perfumes and flowers. (Note: Although cited as *Samājottara*, this is actually *Guhyasamājatantra* 4.19c.)
"The 'flower' is designated as the self-realm (*svadhātu*) of a young woman," as stated in the *Samājottara* and the *Guhyasamājatantra* (18.107ab).

In this context, "new" refers to the lotus of the consort (*vidyā*). Its "newness" consists in its being freshly blossomed; for that [lotus], when its menses have not yet appeared, is fully blossomed and pure. However, it gradually undergoes fading. Regarding the phrase "having made it full of flowers," one should desire her while she is menstruating. As for the non-closure of the lotus, authorities maintain that it lasts for thirteen days following the onset of the menses, specifically from the third day onwards.
There are some women who, even with great effort, do not emit semen; for the sake of avoiding that [failure], this was said.

"Binding the mouth" is for the purpose of ensuring that neither is seen, for if they are seen, a lack of faith is feared. "That which one should cause to fall" refers to the semen. Having pressed the *vajra* with the thumb and ring finger, and having drawn it from the lotus (*padma*), one should insert it directly. The Master and the Wisdom consort, having arisen, should deposit [it] by means of the lotus itself; thus, the secret empowerment is described as the empowerment of the secret parts of both Wisdom and Means.

He speaks of the consecration of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*): "It must be performed. "In that very [place]" means in the case of the student’s consort alone. It is not, however, in the case of a yoginī who has been given by the student for the sake of constant enjoyment, because service toward her is a cause for hell. As it is said: "He who violates the Guru’s bed goes to terrible hells of sin."
Thus it has been said. And it was stated by the Blessed One [in the *Gurupañcāśikā*]:
"The wealth of the guru is like his own life, and his wife is like the guru himself."
With a mind always composed, he should regard his world as being like that of a kinsman.
Out of fear of the sin of destroying a *caitya*, one should not even step over its shadow;
what need is there to mention stepping over sandals, seats, vehicles, and so forth?

For if transgressing even the shadow of one's guru produces sin, then transgressing against the guru’s most beloved wife—who is to be regarded as equal to the guru—produces nothing less than a great sin. Therefore, it is said in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*:
Those men who,
out of great delusion, transgress the shadow of the Guru, his wife, his sandals, or his seat and bed, carry the edge of a razor.
Even when well-instructed, if a disciple should transgress the command of the guru,
he will become a cripple in this world and dwell in hell in the next world.
"Through the employment of deceit and guile, by manifesting false devotion, one is born in the hells and other realms as one afflicted with consumption, leprosy, and great diseases.

Furthermore, that *vidyā* which has been given by the disciple to the Guru specifically for the purpose of the secret consecration (*guhyābhiṣeka*) must be used by the Guru himself and then bestowed upon the disciple; and in that [consecration], the disciple should experience the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*). Thus it is said in the *Samājottara*:
Extremely faithful, of great wisdom, beautiful, and dear to the practitioner; having practiced the rites of the single yoga, she is indeed a *samayin* of the *samaya*.
The practitioner must indeed bestow the sacrificial fee upon the teacher;
having been empowered by the teacher, it should then be given back to that practitioner.

She by whom a single deity-yoga has been practiced together with the practitioner, and by whom a single ritual action—the cultivation characterized by meditative absorption and performance—has been practiced, is one who has practiced the single ritual action of yoga (*ekayogakriyābhyastā*). For a practitioner in the form of Vairocana or another [deity], the *samayinī* (pledge-consort) is one who conforms to his own family (*svakula*). However, in the absence of such [a consort], she should be understood as this *samayinī* precisely through the practice of the single ritual action of yoga. "Right" means not crooked. Indeed, the "left" one should entice her once she has been brought near.

Having himself empowered it and partaken of it, the Guru should then give it to the practitioner; for in this way, it becomes empowered. "Equal flavor" (*samarasam*) means innate bliss (*sahajasukha*). "Within the sphere of the disciple" means that which is to be personally experienced by the disciple. As for the practice here, it should be understood from the mouth of the Guru through the specific performance of what has been taught at the time of the radiation of the *bodhicitta*, free from conceptual constructions such as subject and object. As it is said in the *Dvikalpa* [Hevajratantra II.iii.22]:
"But when the moment of supreme bliss, devoid of multiplicity, is attained..."

The Teacher would say: "O Mahāsattva, that which is to be maintained (*dhāraṇīya*) is great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Here, supreme joy (*paramānanda*) is indeed innate joy (*sahajānanda*), because it is distinguished by being devoid of diversity. Its attainment should be understood as occurring precisely through the process of arising; however, once it has arisen, there is no occasion for the teacher’s speech, as it would be useless. "To be maintained" means to be firmly grasped. In this context, those who propound the doctrine of direct experience (*samvedanavādin*) declare that very experience of great bliss to be reality (*tattva*). The Mādhyamikas, however, maintain that by means of that [bliss], one declares the inconceivability of all phenomena (*sarvadharmācintyatā*).

Then one should state that very fourth [point]. If it is asked what is meant by that, he says: "It is self-cognized," and so forth. Because the knowledge that has become the fruit—being of equal flavor (*samarasa*) and self-cognized through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—comes into being. The sense is that meditative cultivation is impossible for that which has not been previously perceived. He further qualifies this knowledge as the fruit: it is devoid of the cognition of self and other, because it is free from conceptual constructions such as "to be accepted" or "to be rejected."

For this very reason, it is equal to space (*khasama*) and free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). It is stainless (*viraja*) because of the absence of the two obscurations. It is empty (*śūnya*) and devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), because its essence consists of both existence and non-existence. "Existences" (*bhāva*) refers to things such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth; their "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is their non-arising, and it has that as its essence. Alternatively, "existence" (*bhāva*) is the body of the yogin, and "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is his sensations and so forth; since these two constitute its essence, it is described in that way. It is "supreme" (*para*) because it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). It is "without life-force" (*aprāṇa*) because it is devoid of a living soul (*jīva*) upon separation from that [life-force].

He is the supreme syllable because he is without beginning or end. He is all-pervasive because he consists of the *bodhicitta* of all phenomena. He possesses the wisdom of a Buddha because of his union with the five wisdoms, such as the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and others, in the forms of Vairocana and the rest. He is Śrī Heruka because, through the perfection of non-dual wisdom, he is free from the superimposition of cause, intrinsic nature, and effect.

For this very reason, he states with the words beginning "bhāva" that the universe arises from the causal tantra of the *bodhicitta*, because [the universe] originates from the afflictions and karma whose nature is that [same *bodhicitta*]. "Bhāva" (existence) refers to the gross form of the body, as it is the object of worldly convention regarding existence even among children. "Abhāva" (non-existence) refers to subtle entities consisting of the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*). By way of illustration, the intermediate category of speech (*vāṅmaya*) should also be understood. Thus, the body, speech, and mind have been described; as have the other six sense faculties.

By the phrase "those which," the stable [elements] such as earth and so forth, as well as the moving sentient beings, are referred to. And thus it is said in the *Dvikalpa* (Hevajratantra I.viii.38–39a):
"The inferior is the subtle object, while the superior is called 'existence' (*bhāva*)."

Excluding the middle one from the two [extremes], the others are the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*). Those which are stable or moving—through the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of these [faculties] such as existence (*bhāva*) and so forth, their state of being composed of great bliss (*mahāsukhamayatva*) is established. For it is the very mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) that appears in those various forms, as in a dream; thus, since it is composed of bliss, their being composed of that [bliss] is already established, just as waves are composed of water when the water is cold. This is the intended meaning.

For this very reason, he says "Bliss," and so forth, to show that from this very *bodhicitta*, the four joys (*ānanda*) consisting of it radiate forth. The "Hero" (*vīra*) is the practitioner (*sādhaka*), because he has initiated vigor for the sake of reaching the further shore for both himself and others. That very [joy] is "Bliss" (*ānanda*), because it is impossible for anything other than bliss to be the enjoyer of happiness. "Supreme Bliss" (*paramānanda*) is the "Yoginī," because she is sought after for the sake of the bliss of sexual union (*surata*). "Bliss of Sexual Union" (*suratānanda*) is "Cessation Bliss" (*viramānanda*), because it is the bliss of sexual union in its distinguished form.

"Entirety" (*samasta*) refers to the form of wisdom and means, because at that time the intentions of the woman and man are equal; or, because it serves as the meeting place for the hero and yoginī who possess the forms of bliss and supreme [bliss]. "Having that bliss as its means" (*tatsukhopāya*) means that the bliss of sexual union (*suratānanda*) is the means, the immediate cause, for this [state]. And he is both "the means of that bliss" and "all-knowing" (*sarvavit*), because the Blessed One is of the nature of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).

He speaks of their form in order to characterize it, beginning with "the first" and so forth. *Ānandamātra* is unexalted, a mild pleasure characterized by the presence of the conceptualization of subject and object through embracing, kissing, and so on; it consists of the intense longing for touch between the lotus and the vajra, occurring again and again until the friction of the vajra and lotus.
[As stated in the *Hevajratantra* II.iii.13:
"Having embraced with both arms a Prajñā of sixteen years..."

"Because of the union of the bell and the vajra, the consecration by the master (ācārya) is intended"—this is taught in the *Dvikalpa*. Furthermore, supreme joy (*paramānanda*) is characterized by the desire for ever-increasing bliss; it is superior to [ordinary] joy and consists of the enjoyment of the knowledge of inverted bliss, taking the form of its fruition (*vipāka*). It is called "cessation" (*virama*) because it is free from the two conceptualizations of subject and object, which have become attenuated. Regarding the term "cessation" (*virama*): because of the cessation of passion in the form of the desire for bliss, the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*) arises, culminating in the disappearance of all mental effort (*ābhoga*).

This observation of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is an indicative mark; it consists of the stage of "consummation" (*vimarda*), which is the state of intensity characterized by the thought "this bliss has been enjoyed by me," accompanied by the conceptual construction that grasps the form of the passion for bliss, and which lasts until that [grasping] ceases. As it is said in the *Dvikalpa*:
"The third is so called because of the destruction of passion."

The fourth is the "innate" (*sahaja*), which is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). It consists of conventional bodhicitta, is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), is the experience of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). For this very reason, it is devoid of attachment to pleasure and devoid of adherence to its opposite. As it is said in the *Hevajratantra* (II.iii.8cd):
"It is characterized by the absence of [dualistic] marks, distinct from the [other] three, and free from both passion and dispassion."

Is this, then, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)? It is not so; for it is obtained through specific skillful means (*upāyaviśeṣa*), and through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the Guru. If it were obtained by its own inherent nature (*svarasataḥ*), it would be so [automatically]. This very thing they call "consolation" (*āśvāsa*). Because of the identity (*tādātmya*) of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) and the knowledge of emptiness (*jñānaśūnyatā*), which are mutually sealed (*parasparamudrita*), and because they have the form of Akṣobhya-Vajradhara, one will certainly become a Tathāgata and a Vajradhara through the attainment of that path. Therefore, O Sovereign of the Gods, the preceptor’s initiation becomes supreme.
I shall now speak of the supreme secret initiation; listen with reverence.
When bliss remains firmly established for even a single moment in the secret place, [that is the secret initiation].
Then the secret [teaching] is fully explained; otherwise, it would be merely worldly.
I shall now describe the initiation of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*), which is difficult to obtain everywhere.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is said to have the nature of semen (*śukra*), and knowledge (*jñāna*) is remembered as consisting of bliss.
Empowerment is the swift downfall; the state of gnosis is otherwise bliss;
its cessation is called the fourth, characterized by innate gnosis.

Now, he shows that following the fourth consecration comes the granting of permission (*anujñādāna*), beginning with the words "Bodhi," and so forth. The fourth is the consecration of the *bodhicitta*. Regarding the phrase "the wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra*): by substituting the words "Vajra," "Ratna," "Padma," "Karma," and "Śabda" in place of "Dharma," one should recite [the mantra] five times in succession while the disciple meditates on each respective Tathāgata. However, when meditating on Vajrasattva, the granting of permission consists of the verse beginning with "Prajñā. Birth becomes fruitful through the attainment of the consecrations.
Life is fruitful because it is suitable for performing the welfare of others; birth in the family of the Buddhas occurs precisely on the stage of the Joyous (pramuditā-bhūmi).

Now, however, by means of the four empowerments (*abhiṣeka*), [the results] are described according to their respective fitness (*yogyatā*) based on the *Vajrasattvasaṃvarodaya*. Deliverance, the state of perfection, awakening, and the abandonment of the latent tendencies of desire for other [states] are to be understood precisely through that same fitness. The destruction of attachment pertains to material things. "Beneficial" (*hita*) means wholesome for the future. "Well-disposed" (*suprasāda*): this is the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), namely, that one who has been consecrated according to the ritual rules is impelled toward excellence alone by all the Buddhas with well-disposed minds, as if toward a beloved son.

The connection is: "by your power. The explanation of this is: "I shall accomplish," and so forth. This is the foundation (*pratiṣṭhāna*). It is worshipped even by all the foremost Great Bodhisattvas. It is joined with that very word. "Consecration" (*abhiṣeka*) refers to the three consecrations. "Having understood" means by means of signs such as the brightening of the face and the arising of horripilation. The "jewel of consecration" is the fourth, because it extends unsurpassed delight.

Thus, here, for the sake of those of superior capacity, the procedure for the mandala initiation has been briefly elucidated. However, it should be understood that it has been described by us in detail in the *Vajrāvalī-maṇḍalopayikā*.
% R Vajrāvalī

Thus, having obtained the ultimate consecration of the accumulations (*saṃbhṛti*), he speaks with the words beginning with "he who" and "in the supreme," in order to engage [the disciple] in the conduct for the sake of accomplishing the state of Vajrasattva. The meaning is: for the enjoyment of the unsurpassed perfection of the Holder of the Vajra; for the purification of the field of sentient beings (*sattvakṣetra*) which is the perfection of [his own] enjoyment; and for the grasping of the field of the vessel (*bhājanakṣetra*), such as the perfection of the ground made of wish-fulfilling trees and jewels; thus, he has received the fourth consecration.

The armor is precisely the bodhicitta itself, which is cultivated as being fully comprised within the six perfections. Having placed the vast jewel-mind of consecration upon enlightenment here, because it accomplishes the perfect attainment of the welfare of oneself and others, one should "practice" the bodhicitta; that is to say, one should cultivate it. By this, the cultivation to be described below is indicated. It is stainless because it is free from laziness and the like, and because it is devoid of the turbidity of the stains of transgressions.

For there are two classes of transgressions for one who observes the *saṃvara* of Vajrasattva, known as root transgressions (*mūlāpatti*) and gross transgressions (*sthūlāpatti*). Among these, [the root transgressions are]: disrespecting the guru; violating the command of the Tathāgata; revealing the faults of a vajra-brother out of hatred; abandoning loving-kindness; reviling the three vehicles; disclosing secrets to those who are not yet ripened; reviling the five aggregates which are of the nature of the Tathāgata; doubting the natural purity of all phenomena; and conceptualizing a beginning, middle, or end regarding all phenomena, which are empty of beginning, middle, and end.

The fourteen root downfalls are: the abandonment of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), the defiling of a faithful mind, the failure to observe the commitments as they have been received, and the disparagement of women. Furthermore, there are eight gross downfalls: the forcible appropriation of a *yoginī*, the forcible appropriation of her *bodhicitta*, the failure to conceal what is secret, quarreling regarding the commitments, teaching perverted doctrines to those who are faithful, dwelling for seven nights with those belonging to the vehicle of the listeners (*śrāvaka-yānika*), the conceit of being a yogi without knowing yoga, and teaching the Dharma to those who lack faith.

One who abides in the vow of Vajrasattva must avoid [such conduct] on all sides. Furthermore, one should not—out of a hope for the yoga of the innate, the inconceivable, and so forth—engage in conduct as one pleases during a lower stage than the state of directly realizing the condition of non-duality; for one would then exist merely in outward ostentation, like a rotten *kuṣmāṇḍa* fruit within.
For this very reason, due to the absence of laziness and other such faults, he possesses the yoga of reality with uninterrupted excellence.
Because the consecration of the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*) is explained as being primary, the treatise is likewise [structured]. This refers to the second ritual manual (*kalpa*).
The fifth cluster in the *Āmnāyamañjarī*.
